doc.title: Dave Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: New Orleans, Chicago and San Francisco trad styles
summary: He describes brass band, classic New Orleans, revival, Chicago and San Francisco styles and the tuba versus string bass question.

blocks.x: Can you pinpoint what’s the major difference between those traditional jazz styles? Is it in the rhythm section or is it in the horn ensemble playing?

Well both. So for instance we have — there’s various terms and there’s a lot of disagreement of course, of these various styles. But my view, which sort of forms the basis of this traditional jazz curriculum kit that I’ve developed, is that I think most people in the traditional jazz community would agree that there’s at least three sort of main branches of what we call traditional jazz or Dixieland. There’s a New Orleans branch, a Chicago branch and a San Francisco branch. Most people would agree although even some musicians are really not hip to what those differences are. But basically the New Orleans sound, you’ve got I think two aspects of that or really three if you count the brass band sound as a style, and I do, I think that’s one sound — a whole bunch of horns, no piano, no banjo, separate snare and bass drum, tuba, just a big loud raucous, joyous, kick- up-your-heels and celebrate kind of sound. Then we have the early recordings that are in the classic New Orleans style that Louis Armstrong Hot Fives, the Jelly Roll Morton Red Hot Peppers, King Oliver’s Creole Jazz Band, etc. That’s a very rather structured kind of style, a very tightly, kind of a tightly knit ensemble, a very rough texture but organized. And then we have the later what I call the New Orleans revival style which came to prominence in the forties with people like George Lewis and Bunk Johnson, and that’s a

more loose, kind of a laid back sound, a little more rough and ragged but very much from the heart. It’s almost like a folk music. It tells a story. It’s played right from the heart and it doesn’t concern itself overly with European conventions, the classical European tradition as far as pitch and intonation and so forth. It’s all about how can I tell a story. And then you have the Chicago style, which is more smooth and swingy kind of a feel, more maybe technically accomplished playing, a little bit more cerebral, and then you have the San Francisco branch which kind of harks back to the classic New Orleans style but with a twist. It’s very brassy and it’s very two-beat. It’s kind of an um-chick um- chick instead of a bump-bump-bump-bump. Very insistent kind of swaggering rhythm. Just a very distinctive sound. Banjo and tuba instead of string bass.
I was just going to ask, it’s always seemed to me that whether you have a tuba or if you have a string bass really changes the music.

Um hum. Although there are tuba players who can walk fours very well on tuba, and even some bands playing San Francisco style have used the string bass playing mostly on one and three. So it can be done either way. But yeah, that does generally change the character of the music.
